claims.text: The FeNiCrCoCu coating and Cu matrix begin as perfect single crystals without pre-existing defects.
Above 900 K, the friction spike and loss of wear resistance are caused by stacking-fault annihilation followed by localized amorphization.
Thermal activation causes stacking faults to collapse and Shockley partial dislocations to annihilate.
The annihilation of Shockley partials produces dislocation starvation.
Above 900 K, thermal energy exceeds the relevant stacking-fault energy barrier.
Dislocation starvation destabilizes the FeNiCrCoCu lattice.
The destabilized FCC lattice transforms locally into an amorphous structure at the contact or sliding interface.
The resulting amorphous layer has high shear compliance and low yield strength.
High shear compliance and low yield strength increase the real contact area and cause the friction coefficient to spike.
The amorphous layer lacks strain-hardening capacity, causing rapid material removal and loss of wear resistance.
Friction and wear increase sharply between 900 K and 1200 K.
The sharp friction and wear change coincides with a decrease in FCC atom fraction and an increase in amorphous atom fraction in the contact zone.
At lower temperatures, the crystalline coating undergoes gradual thermal softening rather than a phase change or friction spike.
The baseline response is a linear decrease in elastic modulus and hardness with increasing temperature.
The proposed mechanism applies only at an indentation depth of 30 Å because surface-to-volume effects dominate there.
The Cu matrix remains elastic and does not contribute to the plastic deformation zone.
The temperature threshold for amorphization depends on the interatomic potential and strain-rate sensitivity.
Some HEAs exhibit improved elevated-temperature wear resistance because of protective oxide formation.
A vacuum MD simulation lacks the atmospheric oxidation mechanism that can improve high-temperature wear resistance.
A friction spike that correlates with dislocation-density reduction without an increase in amorphous atom fraction would falsify the amorphization-driven mechanism.

contradictions.description: The rule treats absence of a friction spike when amorphous fraction remains low as falsifying the amorphization mechanism. That result is actually consistent with the proposed claim that amorphization is necessary for the spike; only a spike without amorphization would directly contradict it.

The baseline asserts a linear decrease in modulus and hardness with temperature, but the motivating conditions specify a non-monotonic 600 K response involving reduced dislocation density and increased elastic modulus. The hypothesis does not reconcile this lower-temperature behavior with its stated linear baseline.
